security_review.reason: This slice's entire purpose is correcting the serialization guarantee of a privilege-boundary bootstrap for two cluster-global, BYPASSRLS-capable roles. Its design (revised across two codex review rounds, slice doc SS9.4/SS9.5) is TWO-LAYER, not single-mechanism: an unconditional pg_advisory_xact_lock (works for any role, guarantees same-database serialization everywhere) taken before a cluster-wide LOCK TABLE upgrade attempt that deliberately runs in a DEGRADED, unserialized-beyond-same-database mode on the confirmed-real production host (DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL never grants superuser). Security round must specifically verify: (1) the exception handler catches ONLY insufficient_privilege (SQLSTATE 42501) around the LOCK TABLE statement -- any broader WHEN clause (e.g. WHEN OTHERS) would silently swallow unrelated failures and must be rejected; (2) the RAISE WARNING text is unconditionally emitted on that specific failure and is not itself gated behind some condition that could suppress it; (3) SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE is the mode actually used for LOCK TABLE, not a stronger mode that would newly block ordinary GRANT/REVOKE cluster-wide, nor a weaker mode that would not self-conflict; (4) the two pg_advisory_xact_lock calls (chat_definer: 1667525739/cdlk, restored to its original key; job_definer: 1784966251/jdlk, new) are taken UNCONDITIONALLY, before and outside the LOCK TABLE exception-handled block -- never skippable, never inside the same catch; (5) neither file's attributes, fail-closed checks, or (chat_definer) re-pointing guard changed; (6) each of the FOUR concurrency test cases genuinely exercises real concurrency (two distinct connections, Promise.all/allSettled, not sequential awaits) against its OWN claimed lock, not the other one -- the two cross-database cases (job_definer, chat_definer) must fail if their own LOCK TABLE statement is removed; the two same-database degraded-fallback cases (job_definer, chat_definer) must fail if their own pg_advisory_xact_lock statement is removed, NOT if LOCK TABLE is removed (LOCK TABLE is already failing in their degraded scenario, so mutating it proves nothing about them) -- ask the implementer to demonstrate all four via the two separate, correctly-targeted mutation-test rounds named in slice doc SS9.5; (7) the degraded-privilege test cases (the single-caller warning proof, plus both same-database fallback cases) actually connect as a non-superuser role shaped like DigitalOcean's documented doadmin attributes, not merely assert the warning text without exercising the real permission boundary; (8) both racing connections in the same-database fallback cases are pre-created against an ALREADY-EXISTING target role (not a hidden/absent one) before the timed race begins, so PostgreSQL's own CREATE ROLE unique-index race cannot be the accidental source of the observed serialization (slice doc SS9.5 item 1).

_note: Authored 2026-08-05 in an authoring-only session (no register, no worktree, no implementation), then revised the same day after owner review resolved the production-privilege question. Two rounds of live experimentation informed this contract. Round 1 (mechanism selection, slice doc S5): two of the three candidates named in the already-merged deferral (docs/autopilot-chat-definer-role-provisioning.md SS10 item 8) were tested against this session's local Postgres 16 cluster and found NOT to work as documented -- SERIALIZABLE isolation does not detect the cross-database conflict, and a row-level FOR UPDATE lock on a shared catalog row does not block cross-database despite the catalog's storage being physically shared. The chosen mechanism (relation-level LOCK TABLE) was cross-checked for three separate properties: that it blocks cross-database (it does), that it does not block ordinary GRANT/REVOKE elsewhere (it does not), and what privilege it requires (confirmed superuser-only via three separate negative tests). Round 2 (production-privilege resolution, slice doc S5.4.1/S5.4.2), triggered by owner feedback confirming DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL never grants superuser: built a scratch role mirroring doadmin's own documented attribute set (fetched from DigitalOcean's own docs, not assumed) and ran the full bootstrap sequence under it end to end, which both confirmed the fail-open design works as intended AND surfaced a second, previously-unconsidered finding -- PostgreSQL 16 auto-grants a CREATEROLE-holding creator membership in any role it creates, a side effect invisible in every environment this repo runs today because the real credential there is a true superuser. All scratch roles, tables, and databases created during both rounds of experimentation were dropped before this manifest was authored.
